item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports grounding recommendation judgments in observable evidence, while treating automatic labels as imperfect. Penha et al. (2025; revised 2026) find richer metadata and longer histories improve LLM–human agreement, but item-level agreement remains moderate; strong aggregate agreement does not establish individual recommendation usefulness. [Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.23312). Vardasbi et al. (2026) show that auditable historical interaction evidence improves music-search judgments beyond semantic reasoning alone, although this is adjacent evidence rather than validation of purchase usefulness. [Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01040). Liu et al. (2025) find implicit user feedback informative but noisy, with mixed benefits from using feedback content for learning. [Study](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.133/).\n\nPractical synthesis for this task: annotate separate dimensions—“merely related” when evidence establishes topical similarity; “supported current purpose” only when recent history or explicit feedback supports a specific need; “overlapping purchase” only when item evidence or feedback establishes duplication or substitution; “insufficient information” when compatibility, intent, or additional value cannot be established. These are proposed operational labels, not a published validated taxonomy. Attach history item IDs, timestamps, title/description excerpts, and available feedback to every judgment; semantic similarity alone cannot establish redundancy or purchase intent. Abstention research supports explicitly evaluating decisions to withhold unsupported judgments. [Survey](https://aclanthology.org/2025.tacl-1.26/). Use the 20 users’ feedback for exploratory calibration: inspect disagreements, revise rubric examples, and report agreement plus abstention coverage. Keep these diagnostics separate from benchmark HR@10; infer no diversity/conformity traits, ownership, or missing product attributes."}
